title: Magha Puja again
hook: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind

segments.voice: Yesterday, Losar: the scrubbed house, the pinch of barley thrown up, the Great Prayer. Your line was a fresh year. Did your corner get cleaned, and did your wish get said? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-four.

A Chan monk lives up in the branches of a pine tree, so the story goes, and people call him the Bird's Nest master. One day a governor named Bai Juyi, who is also a poet, comes and stands underneath. He calls up: that's a dangerous place to sit. The monk calls down: your seat is more dangerous than mine. Then the governor asks the big question. What is the heart of the Buddha's teaching? And the monk in the tree answers with a verse this path has met before. Today is Magha Puja, the full moon of that verse.
screen: `A MONK IN A PINE TREE.` → `YOUR SEAT IS MORE DANGEROUS.` → `WHAT IS THE HEART OF IT?`

segments.voice: Begin with the full moon. In Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, Magha Puja remembers a gathering of monks and the short teaching the Buddha gave them. One of its verses sits in the Dhammapada, and in Max Müller's words it reads: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." You've walked around a temple with that verse before. This year brought two more homes for it. Second, the Abhidhamma, where this year began. The Theravada's higher teaching sorts every moment of mind, and its first book opens its list of topics with one sorting: states that are skillful, states that are unskillful, and states that are neither. The Pali for skillful is kusala, the same word that stands behind Müller's to do good. So the middle of the Magha Puja verse is also the first cut the Abhidhamma makes. Third, Chan. In Chinese tradition the verse is called the shared precept of the seven Buddhas, which tradition says each Buddha of the past taught. Which brings us back to the tree. The Bird's Nest master gives the governor the verse: do no evil, do good. The governor is unimpressed. A child of three knows that, he says. And the monk answers, in the story as the Chan records keep it: a child of three may be able to say it, but an old man of eighty can't manage to do it. That's the turn. The verse isn't hard to understand. A full moon, a book of the mind, a monk in a pine tree all agree on that. It's hard to do, every day, and that's why each school keeps coming back to it as the heart of it.
screen: `ONE VERSE ON THE FULL MOON.` · `SKILLFUL, UNSKILLFUL, NEITHER.` · `THE PRECEPT OF THE SEVEN BUDDHAS.` · then, large: `EASY TO SAY, HARD TO DO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: do all three today. Start the third one now, the mind. Sit, and let the breath settle like a glass of water left alone. When it's a little clearer, choose the first: one small harm you'll skip today. Make it child-sized, something a three-year-old could understand. Then the second: one small good thing you'll actually do, also child-sized. Then let both rest, and come back to the clearing water. The verse was easy to say. The bell holds the time.
Magha Puja. The full moon remembering the gathering of monks and the verse: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind, carried by Theravada, the Abhidhamma and Chan alike. Today's word.
Your line: the heart of it. Tonight, check the child-sized harm you skipped and the child-sized good you did, and give the old man of eighty a nod. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: In Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, Buddhists keep Magha Puja on a full moon with temple visits, giving, precepts and an evening candlelit walk around the temple, often chanting the verses of the Ovada Patimokkha.

options: nothing; you bow and walk away.

original.note: Pali kusala: skillful, wholesome; the 'do good' of Dhammapada 183 and the Abhidhamma's first sorting word.

trapdoor: what you thought: Magha Puja is a Thai full-moon holiday.
what it means: the full moon of one short verse, avoid evil, do good, purify the mind, carried by several schools.
what a scholar hears: kusala in Dhammapada 183, the kusala triad opening the Dhammasangani's matrix, and the Bird's Nest story in the Chan lamp records.

notes: Index title has no word; word kept as 'Magha Puja again'.
Dhammapada 183 quoted from Müller (1881), same wording as day 694; confirm.
Dhammasangani's matika opens with the triad kusala / akusala / abyakata; 'neither' renders abyakata (indeterminate). Confirm the plain-language phrasing.

Bird's Nest (Niaoke Daolin) and Bai Juyi story paraphrased; the 'child of three' and 'old man of eighty' numbers are from the story itself. Confirm the source (Jingde Chuandeng Lu, fascicle 4) and that 'your seat is more dangerous' is a fair paraphrase.
'Shared precept of the seven Buddhas' (qifo tongjie ji) and 'said by every Buddha of the past' reflect the tradition's own claim, not a historical one; confirm phrasing.
Avoided the gathering's traditional count of monks per the claims rule.
Original: Pali kusala in Devanagari (कुसल); confirm.

Editor: fixed 'its first verse' — in the Ovada Patimokkha (DN 14) the khanti verse (Dhp 184) comes first, so Dhp 183 is now 'one of its verses'; seven-Buddhas claim framed as tradition; 'a verse you know' and 'turns into to do good' reworded.
